rationale: Clinical ginger extracts and powders give mixed or inconclusive anxiety results, and the Parkinson extract trial has no posted results. Aqueous and ethanolic rhizome extracts increased open-arm time in small animal experiments, with differing locomotor reporting. The measured behavior and preparations leave the clinical effect of eating grated ginger unresolved.

Mean fatigue severity rose 3.7 points in 14 Parkinson study completers after three months of brewed green tea. The same-cohort thesis contains no participant-level paired scores or exact fatigue p-value. This gives a minimal descriptive worsening lean in the exact setting with no control. A postoperative randomized comparison found less fatigue with brewed tea in a different setting.

Topical ground-clove gel reduced needle pain, and topical extracted eugenol gave favorable descriptive toothache relief. The older mouse ground-powder test reported no analgesic effect, with dose and route details limited. Injected oil and oral aqueous extract studies report animal nociceptive effects. Ground clove ingestion and clinical Parkinson pain remain unresolved.
